commentBody: Enjoyed this. Some nice friction
Caitlin, thank you for the link about the last edition of the Momma comic strip.  I didn't know that story, and I found it very moving.
This was a nice one! If I had correctly remembered how to spell an author’s name I might’ve had my best Saturday time in a while!

Woot! Fun and tough… And I get it. Well I’m happy with my 24 minutes or so, they got it done in nine minutes. That’s OK. This was challenging on the right side. I did it with no help. That makes my night.

A pleasant puzzle mostly with clues that were closer to an easy Friday than any Saturday.To balance those, I had a lot of trouble with a) the NE corner and b) how to correct my SHOOKETy / SASy crossing. If finally dawned that "ukitar" was a hint to the answer, especially after GUITuLELE didn't work.

Really enjoyable puzzle that took me awhile to get started, but which came together nicely.  Lots of fun entries including OSCARSPEECH, GAMETABLE, and EMPTYSUIT.

TIL that there’s a portmanteau instrument called a GUITALELE.  I had also never encountered SHOOKETH.  And although I’ve learned to fill in aro when called upon, it took me a minute to see that it was short for AROMANTIC — a classic example of me learning something in crossword land without actually understanding it.

I was surprised to remember that Mell Lazarus drew MOMMA, but even more surprised to learn that he did so for 46 years.  That was one of the funnies that I always skipped, along  with Family Circus.

Ha, I read 23A as “the very first one was WORN by a ventriloquist”.
BELT? SASH? CAPE? WIRE??

Next wondered, for 2.5 seconds, how a ventriloquist would wear an EMMY.

After a really challenging Friday (which took me about 24 hours of simmering on it), I enjoyed this puzzle a lot! Still quite a bit of resistance for me, but solvable. I understand the more seasoned crossword-ers may have found it to be easy, but I’m still pleased with myself. 

After about 2 years of solving, this is my first time achieving an 8 day streak… hoping to complete my first full week straight (Mon-Sun) of gold stars if I am lucky tomorrow! 🍀
I think they switched Friday and Saturday this week.

This puzzle was dressed to the nines, in a way, with 14 answers of that length.  Many of them added personality to the box – I’LL SHUT UP, GUITALELE, SMART MOVE, PAPA BEAR, EMPTY SUIT.

There are 20 longs, actually – answers of eight letters or more – extremely high for a 15x15, and Hanna’s grid-building chops show, as there’s hardly a whiff of junk to be found, IMO.  This grid design, by the way, is a Times puzzle debut.

I loved the SAW SHARK touching corners with the WHALES, and the symmetrical LIGHTEN UP and TEE HEE HEE. I adored GUITALELE, a word I’ve never seen or heard before, and which is so much fun to say.

There was enough vagueness in the cluing to get my brain fully involved, and yet, as with all of Hannah’s puzzles, it had a lovely soft feel overall.

And thus, I was charmed and delighted.  This was a gift – thank you, Hannah!
Too easy for a Saturday, but enjoyable nonetheless.
In terms of difficulty, they should have swapped Friday's and Saturday's puzzles.

A fine puzzle! 

The bear documentaries I’ve seen on TV (quite a few, actually) would lead me to conclude that the picture with the column most likely depicts a mama bear. The mamas are always protecting their cubs from the males. But then that would contradict the Goldilocks story…
There’s surely a bear expert among the commenters who might set me straight!

The sauna salesmen were full of hot air.

(They got into heated arguments.)

This one was tough for me because my mind kept latching on to certain scenarios and not budging – *earthquakes* for "this might be felt" and *unassembled* for "like much IKEA furniture" (and then trying to find synonyms that would fit.) The puzzle itself was great; it was my own mind that was fighting me. And so it was a funny solve, one of many duhs and ahas spoken out loud whenever I filled in an entry. Thank you, Hannah, for a fine Saturday puzzle! ............................. Today I'm not referencing the puzzle for a musical accompaniment. I'm straight up honoring Duncan Sheik who passed away. (With 6 degrees of separation, I'm sure there's something in the puzzle that would have something to do with his music...) Though he's famous for "Barely Breathing," I'm linking instead to my favorite song from that same album: https://youtu.be/Q-Fy5Lh4yME?is=YaXulYrK9oUK_VAT (RIP)

Good puzzle, though maybe not quite Saturday material. I went into the grid primed for pushback after yesterday’s chewy serving, but it yielded rather quickly. All but a couple of the clues  were inferable; no general knowledge really required. 

Not a single-digit solve, but it is still a half hour shy of sunrise here. 

There’s been a lot of talk of The Great Easening lately. And here I had hoped it was just the SATs.

Sorry if this was already asked but does anyone know how to access this puzzle in the app? I have a separate account for the NYT and I saw this notice:

The New York Times regularly publishes special crosswords for subscribers. The puzzles are designed to have the difficulty of an early-week grid and to use the theme throughout. The title of this puzzle, “Times Past,” celebrates 175 years of The Times. It was constructed by Sam Ezersky and Anna Kaufman.

Yesterday's puzzle ultimately defeated me after an hour long fight. I found today's grid even harder - having stared at it for 30 minutes I had typed in maybe 20 entries and that was that: further progress seemed impossible. So I checked the puzzle - almost everything I had entered was actually correct, which was my only (minor) victory today. Next I revealed my personal arcana, which allowed me to continue the solve, but only with further, occasional checks. This is what the grid looked like for me, in the end: https://imgur.com/a/F5UFbUt Sometimes I am able to complete properly hard Saturday puzzles, but only under specific circumstances: when there aren't too many personal unknowns and when clues rely on misdirection rather than opaqueness. Today I knew almost none of the trivia and Americana - almost all of the names and things like HOME PLATE (as clued) and SENATE PAGES tripped me up big time. Then there were clues I'll describe as opaque for lack of a better word: ones I perceive not as intelligently misdirecting but simply only tenuously connected to their answers: "One might be cut off by an orchestra" and "Sure ... that's true ..." - to me that's the sort of clue that requires a load of crosses, but those are hard to get in a puzzle as difficult as this. I'm not complaining, mind you - obviously I am bound to fail many late-week puzzles at the NYT. I am just describing my process and my difficulties.

I thought I was having a lucky break with IPAD and AROMANTIC in the beginning and then it petered out very quickly. I found this way harder than Friday where I had some traction, though I didn't get close to finishing either, as is usual for me right now. Friday's fill had a lot more "ahh I see! I could have got that" vibe, and this Saturday feels very obscure to me in comparison. So many names and trivia. The long answers are great but they are out of reach for me because of the crosses.
OSCARSPEECH is a nice fill with a clue that I had no clue about, but I can see it hitting the sweet spot for others.
What is PAPABEARS?! Is it a cute nickname for dads? Is it supposed to be the fictional bear-fathers I see on wikipedia?
GAMETABLE is felt as in you touch it when playing on it??

Culty?  CULTY??  Even after I get it, it took a while to get it. Kudos to everyone who found the puzzle easy.  The obscure sports figures stopped me in my tracks, and I struggled with some of the quirkier clues, but when I sorted things out and trusted my gut, (EAT, for instance, was a keeper), I loved it.

Thank you, Hannah.  Happy week-end to all.
29 down is weak

I've previously expressed a dislike for multiple-word answers that aren't actual phrases, but are just words that are often said together by some people in some situations. "I MEAN YEAH" is definitely one of those. They're clearly a necessity coming from American puzzles having so few blocks, and needing repetitive 3-/4-letter words, wacky proper nouns, abbreviations & acronyms, incomplete phrases, and these non-phrasal groups of words just to be able to fill the grid.
I'm getting used to it the more I do American puzzles though, and I wouldn't use the word "dislike" anymore. In fact I'd probably call these filler categories "quirky" or even "charming" now. I've learned a lot about music (REO Speedwagon, the CBGB Club, ETTA James...), sport (BAMA, NATS, RBI...), American geography, schools, politics, food and more!

Whoof. Unfortunately got very little enjoyment out of this one - I am a very strong believer that the best crossword clues are ones that are very difficult to parse when you first read them, but then seem clear as day once you figure out the answer. While the constructor gave it a good effort, ultimately I think the cluing left much to be desired. GAMETABLE has gotten a lot of celebration here, but I think "IT might be felt" is a much better clue with only one word change; the same goes for CULTY and IMEANYEAH. The Southeast corner was also particularly torturous, as pretty much every late night host or SNL alum fits - I tried Conan OBRIEN, Seth MEYERS, Jimmy FALLON, KEENAN Thompson, Johnny CARSON, John OLIVER, James CORDEN, and Graham NORTEN all before I tried Jimmy KIMMEL. When you have crossers that are inane bits of pop trivia (like SHOOKETH) or extremely vague/weak cluing ("I'm in!" or "Saturate") it sort of sucks the fun out of it for me. I saw this as a Gen-Z person who literally saw Christine Sydelko's post when she first said SHOOKETH! This one just needed another run through editing for the cluing.
